line: Hello. Helen Zhou. I'm a GP, and I run the Saturday health talks here. Mostly blood pressure checks.
choice2: Nice to meet you, Dr. Zhou.
choice3: I'm not here for a checkup.

line: Then everyone asks about their cousin's prescriptions. Have you found a doctor here yet, since you moved?
choice2: I go to the clinic on Fifth.
choice3: I'll sort it out. Nice to meet you.

line: Most people your age haven't. Get one before you need one. The clinic on Fifth takes new patients on Mondays, if you call at eight exactly.
choice1: Do people from the center go there?

line: Good. Then you know the waiting room. Bring a book.
choice1: Do people from the center go there?
choice2: I always do. See you, Dr. Zhou.

line: Some. For a lot of the seniors, my table on Saturday is the only time they see a doctor all year. I've asked the clinic to send someone over. They keep saying they'll circle back.
choice1: Why don't the seniors go to the clinic?
choice2: Want me to ask them too?

line: The forms are in English, the phone line puts you on hold, the desk asks questions they don't follow. So they wait until it's bad and go to the emergency room. Or they come here and sit on a folding chair for me.
Not me on my own. I've been talking with Ruth Hale at the library about a joint session. Her volunteers here, our people over there. Some of our board think it's a waste of time.
choice2: I hope it happens. See you.

line: They think if we send people to the library, they won't come back. _shakes her head_ I think they'll come back with their benefits sorted out, and still come for lunch on Tuesday.
choice1: Put people in the same room.

line: Hello. Helen Zhou. I'm a GP, I do the health talks at the center on Grand. Today I'm just here with a patient.
choice2: Nice to meet you, Dr. Zhou.
choice3: I'd rather not chat right now.

line: Mrs. Wu. She won't let anyone else translate for her cardiologist. She's in with him now.
It's not kindness, it's arithmetic. The phone interpreter puts her on hold, she hangs up, and she doesn't come back for a year. A morning of mine is cheaper.
Every week, to someone. The clinic does what it can. Five people at the desk, three hundred patients, one phone line for every language.
choice2: I'll let you get back to Mrs. Wu.

line: Good morning. Sorry, I'm reading the minutes from last night's board meeting. Twice.
Two hours on the festival budget, ten minutes on everything else. I got my ten minutes.
choice2: Good for you. See you later.

line: A joint forum with the library. Ruth Hale's people and ours, one afternoon. Health, benefits, the school forms.

They said they'd think. Mr. Guo said we are not a branch office of the library. He's right that we built this place ourselves. $ [neutral] But the seniors who need it most don't care whose building it is.
choice1: Put people in the same room.

line: Ah, {playerName}. Do you ever have a Monday evening free?
The parks committee meets Mondays at city hall. Nobody from this side of Grand has gone in years.
The benches, the lights on the path, who gets the tables on Saturday mornings. The tai chi group lost the good spot last year because nobody was there to say they exist.
I sit on two committees already and I see patients. And it shouldn't always be me, the one person they think of when they think of us. You ask questions and you listen to the answers. You'd be good.
Good, you're here. Ruth and I are finally doing it.
A health and benefits fair at the library, Saturday. Blood pressure at my table, benefits sign-up at hers. I want people from here walking in through the front door. Will you help me bring them?
choice2: Who are you hoping will come?

line: Mrs. Wu. The Lis from the bakery. Anyone who's been told 'come back with your forms' and didn't. If they walk in with someone they know, they stay.
Hello. Sorry, I'm a little distracted. Phone calls all morning.
Three patients skipped their follow-ups this week. The clinic started asking for ID at the desk.
choice3: I'm sorry. I'll let you work.

line: The clinic says it's for the records. People hear 'ID' and, after the speeches, they hear something else. One of the three is diabetic.

The clinic can't turn you away for not having ID. I'm putting that on a card, Chinese on one side, English on the other, and handing it out on Saturday. I'll know if it worked from his sugar numbers next month.
choice1: I can help hand out the cards.

line: Hello. Good timing. Read this sign for me and tell me if it makes sense.
'You have the right to an interpreter at no cost.' The new rule means the clinic has to offer one, even if it's a phone line.
To you. Mrs. Wu will read 'no cost' and look for the cost. Now I have to make sure people know they can ask, and that asking won't get them in trouble.
I tell them in person, three times. Then I go with the first one who's brave enough. After that they tell each other. Otherwise it's just a sign on the wall.
choice1: I can help spread the word.

line: You're here a lot. I'm glad.
I see you at the center more than anywhere. It's good to see you on this side of Grand too.
Do you come for the lunch, or has Mr. Guo got you on a committee?
Mr. Guo would call it defecting. He's joking. Mostly.
Then you've heard his speech about grants. How the money stops and only we are still here.
choice1: Do you two disagree a lot?

line: About once a week, politely. He built half of this place and I respect that. But don't let it be the only place you go. The clinic, the library, the parks committee. Then bring back what you learn.
Ruth tells me you've become a regular at the library. Good.
Ruth tells me you've become a regular at the library. Good. I hardly see you at the center now.
Her potlucks are better than ours. Don't repeat that. Do people there ask you about the center?

Then tell them. And bring some of that back here, would you? The aunties think the library is for students. If you tell them about the large-print shelf and the tax help, they'll believe you before me.
Hello. I'm in the middle of something.
choice1: I owe you an apology for last time.

line: Accepted. People say worse to me in the waiting room. Come by on Saturday and let me take your blood pressure, that's all.
Not today, I'm finishing a sign-up sheet. Eleven names already.
